claim: Nine mice were trained to explore an elevated square platform surrounded by four walls.
source: Nine mice were trained to explore an elevated square platform surrounded by four walls (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript's Results section describing the experimental setup.

claim: Two distinct visual patterns made from different arrangements of LED strips were attached to two adjacent walls.
source: Two distinct visual patterns (vp1 and vp2) made from different arrangements of LED strips were attached to two adjacent walls.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus used in the study.

claim: A standard cue card attached to one wall remained at the same location throughout the experiment.
source: In addition, a standard cue card attached to one wall remained at the same location throughout the experiment (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes a control element of the experimental design.

claim: Recording sessions included forty 2-min trials alternating between vp1 and vp2 trials.
source: Recording sessions included forty 2-min trials alternating between vp1 and vp2 trials (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Most recording sites were in the MEC (63.0%, 34 out of 54).
source: Histological analysis revealed that the final locations of most recording sites were in the MEC (63.0%, 34 out of 54; Figure 1c–d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of recording sites.

claim: Half of the remaining recording sites were found in the PaS (16.7%, 9 out of 54).
source: Half of the remaining recording sites were found in the PaS (16.7%, 9 out of 54).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of recording sites.

claim: 82.4% (28 out of 34) of recording sites in the MEC had entered layer II of the MEC before the end of the experiment.
source: Of the recording sites in the MEC, 82.4% (28 out of 34) had entered layer II of the MEC before the end of the experiment (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of recording sites.

claim: A total of 944 neurons were recorded over 167 recording sessions.
source: A total of 944 neurons were recorded over 167 recording sessions.
evidence: This describes the dataset collected in the study.

claim: Cells with a HD score exceeding 0.4 and a peak firing rate larger than 5 Hz during vp1 or vp2 trials were considered putative HD cells (106 out of 944 neurons).
source: Cells with a HD score exceeding 0.4 and a peak firing rate larger than 5 Hz during vp1 or vp2 trials were considered putative HD cells (106 out of 944 neurons, Figure 1f).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to identify HD cells in the dataset.

claim: Only HD cells with a directional distributive ratio larger than 0.2 were included in further analysis (N = 104).
source: Only HD cells with a directional distributive ratio larger than 0.2 were included in further analysis (N = 104).
evidence: This describes a filtering criterion applied to the HD cell population.

claim: Out of 104 HD cells, 10.6% (N = 11) were conjunctive grid x HD cells and were excluded from the HD cell category, leaving a total of 93 HD cells.
source: Out of 104 HD cells, 10.6% (N = 11) were conjunctive grid x HD cells and were excluded from the HD cell category, leaving a total of 93 HD cells.
evidence: This describes the final HD cell population used in the analysis.

claim: Of the remaining HD cells, 29.0% were speed modulated, 62.3% had significant spatial sparsity scores, and 31.2% were HD selective only.
source: Of the remaining HD cells, 29.0% were speed modulated, 62.3% had significant spatial sparsity scores, and 31.2% were HD selective only (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This describes the functional properties of the HD cell population.

claim: HD cells expressed similar levels of directional tuning during vp1 and vp2 trials.
source: HD cells expressed similar levels of directional tuning during vp1 and vp2 trials.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparisons of HD scores between trial types.

claim: At the population level, HD scores, peak firing rates and mean firing rates of HD cells were not significantly different between the two trial types.
source: At the population level, HD scores, peak firing rates and mean firing rates of HD cells were not significantly different between the two trial types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is based on statistical tests comparing HD cell properties between trial types.

claim: Preferred directions of HD cells were randomly distributed during both trial types.
source: Preferred directions of HD cells were randomly distributed during both trial types (Rayleigh test of uniformity, vp1: test statistic = 0.0931, p=0.4466; vp2: test statistic = 0.0479, p=0.81).
evidence: This is based on Rayleigh tests of uniformity applied to the distribution of preferred directions.

claim: The behavior of mice was comparable between the two different trial types.
source: Moreover, the behavior of mice was comparable between the two different trial types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2g).
evidence: This is based on comparisons of running speed and head angular velocity between trial types.

claim: A substantial proportion of MEC/PaS neurons shows prominent rhythmic activity in the theta frequency band (6–10 Hz).
source: A substantial proportion of MEC/PaS neurons shows prominent rhythmic activity in the theta frequency band (6–10 Hz) (Alonso and García-Austt, 1987; Cacucci et al., 2004; Mizuseki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A large variability in the theta rhythmic activity of HD cells was observed, with a group of HD cells firing rhythmically at theta frequency and a second group showing no clear rhythmic activity in this frequency range.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a large variability in the theta rhythmic activity of HD cells, with a group of HD cells firing rhythmically at theta frequency (Figure 2a) and a second group showing no clear rhythmic activity in this frequency range (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike-time autocorrelations and power spectra of HD cells.

claim: The theta index distribution was best fit by a model with two components.
source: The distribution of theta indices for all HD cells is shown in Figure 3a. The theta index distribution was best fit by a model with two components (see Materials and methods; Gaussian finite mixture models: log-likelihood = 98.25, df = 5, BIC = 173.83).
evidence: This is based on Gaussian finite mixture modeling of the theta index distribution.

claim: These two components corresponded to non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic cells (N = 34 non-rhythmic, N = 59 theta-rhythmic, theta index threshold = 0.07).
source: In line with Alonso and García-Ausst's work (Alonso and García-Austt, 1987), these two components corresponded to non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic cells (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a, N = 34 non-rhythmic, N = 59 theta-rhythmic, theta index threshold = 0.07).
evidence: This is based on Gaussian finite mixture modeling and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The firing rate of 94.1% (32 out of 34) of non-rhythmic HD cells was significantly modulated by theta phase.
source: Even though non-rhythmic HD cells displayed weak theta phase modulation, the firing rate of 94.1% (32 out of 34) of non-rhythmic HD cells was still significantly modulated by theta phase.
evidence: This is based on Rayleigh tests of uniformity applied to spike timing relative to theta phase.

claim: The power at theta frequency in the local field potentials was similar for non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic HD cells.
source: The power at theta frequency in the local field potentials was similar for non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic HD cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, peak theta power: w = 1024.5, p=0.87).
evidence: This is based on analysis of local field potential power spectra.

claim: There was no significant difference between theta indices of cells recorded in hemispheres in which all tetrode tips were located in the MEC compared to those in which some tetrode tips were in the PaS.
source: There was no significant difference between theta indices of cells recorded in hemispheres in which all tetrode tips were located in the MEC compared to those in which some tetrode tips were in the PaS (w = 2433.5, p=0.75).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of theta indices between recording locations.

claim: The HD selectivity and mean firing rate of non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic HD cells during vp1 trials were similar.
source: The HD selectivity and mean firing rate of non-rhythmic and theta-rhythmic HD cells during vp1 trials were similar (Figure 3c, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, HD score: w = 881, p=0.33, mean firing rate: w = 993, p=0.94), demonstrating that theta-rhythmic and non-rhythmic HD cells displayed similar levels of directional tuning.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of HD scores and firing rates between the two cell types.

claim: 10% (6 out of 59) of theta-rhythmic HD cells showed theta-cycle skipping.
source: When using a theta-cycle skipping index of 0.1 as threshold (see Materials and methods), 10% (6 out of 59) of theta-rhythmic HD cells showed theta-cycle skipping.
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike-time autocorrelations.

claim: Theta-cycle skipping in theta-rhythmic HD cells was slightly lower than what had been previously reported in rats.
source: This was slightly lower than what had been previously reported in rats (Brandon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to a previous study in rats.

claim: Only one mixed non-rhythmic/theta-rhythmic pair was found among 17 pairs of HD cells simultaneously recorded on the same tetrode.
source: By analyzing pairs of HD cells simultaneously recorded on the same tetrode (N = 17), we found only one mixed non-rhythmic/theta-rhythmic pair, suggesting that the two cell populations were partially anatomically segregated.
evidence: This is based on analysis of simultaneously recorded cell pairs.

claim: Out of the seven recording sites with non-rhythmic HD cells that were recovered, four were in the MEC.
source: Out of the seven recording sites with non-rhythmic HD cells that were recovered, four were in the MEC (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis of recording sites in a subset of animals.

claim: Three recording sites with non-rhythmic HD cells were in the postrhinal cortex.
source: Interestingly, three recording sites were in the postrhinal cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the postrhinal cortex might also contain non-rhythmic HD cells.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis and suggests a new finding.

claim: 63.4% (59 out of 93) of the HD cells significantly altered their preferred HD between vp1 and vp2 trials.
source: We found that 63.4% (59 out of 93) of the HD cells significantly altered their preferred HD between vp1 and vp2 trials.
evidence: This is based on statistical testing using a shuffling procedure.

claim: 47.3% (44 out of 93) of the HD cells significantly altered their HD score between trial types.
source: Overall, 47.3% (44 out of 93) of the HD cells significantly altered their HD score between trial types.
evidence: This is based on statistical testing using a shuffling procedure.

claim: Non-rhythmic HD cells showed larger changes in preferred HD between vp1 and vp2 trials than theta-rhythmic HD cells.
source: Non-rhythmic HD cells showed larger changes in preferred HD between vp1 and vp2 trials than theta-rhythmic HD cells (Figure 4c, w = 1465, p=0.00012).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of changes in preferred HD between the two cell types.

claim: HD cells located in the presubiculum and anterodorsal thalamic nucleus maintained their firing rate when an animal explored different environments.
source: It was previously shown that HD cells located in the presubiculum and anterodorsal thalamic nucleus maintained their firing rate when an animal explored different environments (Goodridge et al., 1998; Taube and Burton, 1995; Taube et al., 1990b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 40.9% (38 out of 93) of the HD cells significantly altered their mean firing rate in response to changes in visual landmarks.
source: We found that 40.9% (38 out of 93) of the HD cells significantly altered their mean firing rate in response to changes in visual landmarks.
evidence: This is based on statistical testing using a shuffling procedure.

claim: 86.1% (31 out of 36) of non-spatial HD cells had a significant change in preferred direction, HD score or mean firing rate between the vp1 and vp2 trials.
source: Within this population of non-spatial HD cells, 86.1% (31 out of 36) had a significant change in preferred direction, HD score or mean firing rate between the vp1 and vp2 trials.
evidence: This is based on analysis of a subset of HD cells with no significant spatial modulation.

claim: 83.6% (56 out of 67) of the MEC HD cells displayed significant changes in preferred direction, HD selectivity or mean firing rate between trial types.
source: We found that 83.6% (56 out of 67) of the MEC HD cells displayed significant changes in preferred direction, HD selectivity or mean firing rate between trial types.
evidence: This is based on analysis of HD cells recorded from hemispheres with all tetrode tips in the MEC.

claim: No difference in HD scores was observed between vp1 and vp2 trials for HD cells that showed a tuning curve change between trial types.
source: To address whether these two effects could contribute to the differences observed between vp1 and vp2 trials, we analyzed selectively HD cells that showed a tuning curve change between vp1 and vp2 trials. No difference in HD scores was observed between vp1 and vp2 trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on analysis of HD scores for a subset of HD cells.

claim: There was no clear indication of an accumulation of preferred directions toward either vp1 or vp2.
source: Moreover, there was no clear indication of an accumulation of preferred directions toward either vp1 or vp2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the distribution of preferred directions.

claim: 15.1% (14 out of 93, eight non-rhythmic and six theta-rhythmic) of the HD cells were classified as bidirectional.
source: The analysis showed that 15.1% (14 out of 93, eight non-rhythmic and six theta-rhythmic) of the HD cells were classified as bidirectional, with two cells being bidirectional only during vp1 trials, and 6 cells only during vp2 trials.
evidence: This is based on analysis of bidirectionality scores.

claim: The changes in the BD scores between vp1 and vp2 trials were larger than chance levels.
source: The changes in the BD scores between vp1 and vp2 trials were larger than chance levels (Figure 6d; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 14, v = 12, p=0.009).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing using a shuffling procedure.

claim: Non-rhythmic HD cells showed larger changes in their BD score compared to theta-rhythmic cells.
source: Overall, non-rhythmic HD cells showed larger changes in their BD score compared to theta-rhythmic cells (Figure 6e, w = 1366, p=0.004).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of BD score changes between the two cell types.

claim: Computational models of HD cells predict that differences in the preferred directions of HD cells are preserved at all times.
source: Computational models of HD cells predict that differences in the preferred directions of HD cells are preserved at all times.
evidence: This is a statement about predictions from computational models.

claim: Support for these models comes from numerous studies showing coherent rotation of the preferred directions of HD cells in response to landmark manipulations.
source: Support for these models comes from numerous studies showing coherent rotation of the preferred directions of HD cells in response to landmark manipulations (Taube et al., 1990b; Yoganarasimha et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Theta-rhythmic HD cell pairs did not show significant reorganization when visual landmarks were altered.
source: We found that theta-rhythmic HD cell pairs did not show significant reorganization when visual landmarks were altered (Figure 7b, N = 20, preferred HD: v = 65, p=0.14, HD score: v = 72, p=0.23, IFR association: v = 69, p=0.19).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of reorganization scores.

claim: Visual landmark manipulations caused a reorganization of firing associations in non-rhythmic HD cell pairs.
source: In contrast, visual landmark manipulations caused a reorganization of firing associations in non-rhythmic HD cell pairs (N = 9, preferred HD: v = 2, p=0.01, HD score: v = 1, p=0.00781, IFR association: v = 0, p=0.00391).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of reorganization scores.

claim: HTS HD cell pairs did not show significant visually-driven reorganization.
source: HTS HD cell pairs did not show significant visually-driven reorganization (Figure 7e, preferred HD: v = 69, p=0.50, HD score: v = 51, p=0.14, IFR association: v = 67, p=0.44).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of reorganization scores for high-theta synchronous cell pairs.

claim: LTS cell pairs showed significant reorganization when visual landmarks were altered.
source: In contrast, LTS cell pairs showed significant reorganization when visual landmarks were altered (preferred HD: v = 14, p=0.00042, HD score: v = 16, p=0.00065, IFR association: v = 18, p=0.00097).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of reorganization scores for low-theta synchronous cell pairs.

claim: 219 grid cells were recorded during vp1 and vp2 trials.
source: We recorded the activity of 219 grid cells during vp1 and vp2 trials (Figure 8a and Figure 8—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This describes the dataset of grid cells analyzed in the study.

claim: 48.4% (106 out of 219) of the grid cells showed significant changes in map similarity, preferred HD, or average firing rate between the vp1 and vp2 trials.
source: We found that 48.4% (106 out of 219) of the grid cells showed significant changes in map similarity, preferred HD, or average firing rate between the vp1 and vp2 trials (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing using a shuffling procedure.

claim: Firing associations based on instantaneous firing rates were highly preserved between vp1 and vp2 trials for grid cells (r = 0.96).
source: Firing associations based on instantaneous firing rates were highly preserved between vp1 and vp2 trials (Figure 8e, top left panel, r = 0.96).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of instantaneous firing rates.

claim: Pairwise map similarity from the vp1 and vp2 trials was strongly correlated for grid cells (r = 0.95).
source: Likewise, pairwise map similarity from the vp1 and vp2 trials was also strongly correlated (Figure 8e, bottom left panel, r = 0.95).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of pairwise map similarity.

claim: Only HD cells showed significant reorganization of their IFR association and of their firing rate maps between different trial types.
source: Only HD cells showed significant reorganization of their IFR association and of their firing rate maps between different trial types (reorganization of grid cell pairs between vs. within condition for IFR associations: v = 10911, p=0.10; map similarity: v = 10661, p=0.058).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of reorganization scores between grid cells and HD cells.

claim: The firing associations of grid cells were not significantly altered in response to changes in visual landmarks.
source: These findings suggest that the firing associations of grid cells were not significantly altered in response to changes in visual landmarks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant reorganization in grid cell pairs.

claim: HD cells of the MEC/PaS are at the top level of the HD circuit hierarchy.
source: The medial entorhinal cortex and parasubiculum (MEC/PaS) are located at the top of hierarchical ascending HD pathways (Clark and Taube, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous review.

claim: HD cells intermingle with speed cells and grid cells in the MEC/PaS.
source: There, HD cells intermingle with speed cells and grid cells (Sargolini et al., 2006; Boccara et al., 2010; Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A key function of MEC/PaS cells is to compute an estimate of the animal's position in space, which is optimally represented by the activity of modularly organized grid cells.
source: It has been proposed that a key function of these cells is to compute an estimate of the animal's position in space, which is optimally represented by the activity of modularly organized grid cells (McNaughton et al., 2006; Stensola et al., 2012; Herz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and computational models.

claim: The grid cell network is thought to integrate direction and speed of movement using the activity of HD and speed cells, respectively.
source: To keep track of the animal's position during movement, the grid cell network is thought to integrate direction and speed of movement using the activity of HD and speed cells, respectively (McNaughton et al., 2006; Sargolini et al., 2006; Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and computational models.

claim: The MEC/PaS receive important visual and visuospatial inputs from the postrhinal and retrosplenial cortices.
source: The MEC/PaS also receive important visual and visuospatial inputs from the postrhinal and retrosplenial cortices (Wyss and Van Groen, 1992; Burwell and Amaral, 1998; Czajkowski et al., 2013; Koganezawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: A substantial fraction of MEC/PaS neurons encode information about visual patterns or contexts.
source: Indeed, recent studies have established that a substantial fraction of MEC/PaS neurons encode information about visual patterns or contexts (Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016; Diehl et al., 2017; Ismakov et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: In the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and presubiculum the peak firing rate and directional tuning of HD cells were unchanged when an animal explored visually distinct environments.
source: Indeed, in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and presubiculum the peak firing rate and directional tuning of HD cells were unchanged when an animal explored visually distinct environments (Taube et al., 1990b; Yoder et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: HD cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and presubiculum are driven mainly by self-motion cues derived from vestibular, proprioceptive, and motor efference information.
source: These results suggest that, in these two brain regions, HD cells are driven mainly by self-motion cues derived from vestibular, proprioceptive, and motor efference information (Stackman and Taube, 1997; Yoder and Taube, 2014) and the principal effect of visual landmarks on HD cells is to anchor the HD signal to the external world (Skaggs et al., 1995; Yoder and Taube, 2009; Yoder et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies and is supported by citations.

claim: The impact of visual information on MEC/PaS HD cells extends beyond the anchoring mechanism.
source: Our findings demonstrate that the impact of visual information on MEC/PaS HD cells extends beyond this anchoring mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: A significant proportion of HD cells in the MEC/PaS express a conjunctive code for HD, visual landmarks and position.
source: We suggest that a significant proportion of HD cells in the MEC/PaS express a conjunctive code for HD, visual landmarks and position.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: The firing pattern of non-rhythmic HD cells within the MEC/PaS is not strictly controlled by attractor-like network dynamics.
source: In the current study, we found that the firing pattern of non-rhythmic HD cells within the MEC/PaS is not strictly controlled by these attractor-like network dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: The firing associations of non-rhythmic HD cells are malleable and controlled by visual landmarks.
source: This result indicates that the firing associations of non-rhythmic HD cells are malleable and controlled by visual landmarks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: A recent study reported the existence of a population of HD cells in the dysgranular retrosplenial cortex that was controlled by local landmarks.
source: A recent study also reported the existence of a population of HD cells in the dysgranular retrosplenial cortex that was controlled by local landmarks (Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Bidirectional cells in the retrosplenial cortex were recorded simultaneously with classic HD cells that did not change their tuning curves across compartments.
source: Importantly, bidirectional cells were recorded simultaneously with classic HD cells that did not change their tuning curves across compartments, demonstrating that bidirectional HD cells could re-align independently of the main HD system.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a previous study.

claim: Bidirectional cells in the retrosplenial cortex rotated coherently with one another when the animal moved across compartments.
source: Whereas bidirectional cells rotated coherently with one another when the animal moved across compartments, changing the visual landmarks in our experiment caused a reorganization of firing associations within the non-rhythmic HD cell population.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a previous study, contrasted with the current findings.

claim: The HD signal in cortical areas is more heterogeneous than in the anterodorsal thalamus or the presubiculum.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the HD signal in cortical areas is more heterogeneous than in the anterodorsal thalamus or the presubiculum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Theta-rhythmic HD cells showed no reorganization during the experiment.
source: Theta-rhythmic HD cells showed no reorganization during our experiment.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings in the study.

claim: This coherent HD signal could be well suited for providing directional information to grid cells.
source: This coherent HD signal could be well suited for providing directional information to grid cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and computational models.

claim: Computational models of grid cells assume that the HD signal remains coherent.
source: Indeed, computational models of grid cells assume that the HD signal remains coherent, and recordings from grid cells indicates that they do not show major reorganization after visual cue manipulations (Hafting et al., 2005; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and computational models.

claim: The theta modulation of rhythmic HD cells might play an important role in the integration of the HD signal by grid cells.
source: The theta modulation of rhythmic HD cells might also play an important role in the integration of the HD signal by grid cells.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and previous proposals.

claim: It has previously been proposed that the HD signal needs to be transformed into a theta-modulated signal to be used for navigation.
source: It has previously been proposed that the HD signal needs to be transformed into a theta-modulated signal to be used for navigation (Cacucci et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The segregation of HD cell ensembles during individual theta cycles might contribute to grid periodicity.
source: Moreover, the segregation of HD cell ensembles during individual theta cycles might also contribute to grid periodicity (Brandon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An important function of theta-rhythmic HD cells is to provide a directional input to the grid cell network.
source: We therefore suggest that an important function of theta-rhythmic HD cells is to provide a directional input to the grid cell network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and previous studies.

claim: One function of non-rhythmic HD cells might be to act as an interface between visual landmarks and the coherent HD signal.
source: One function of non-rhythmic HD cells might be to act as an interface between visual landmarks and the coherent HD signal (Bicanski and Burgess, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and computational models.

claim: The population activity of landmark-controlled HD cells could contribute to setting the preferred directions of theta-rhythmic HD cells when an animal enters visually distinct environments.
source: This way, the population activity of landmark-controlled HD cells could contribute to setting the preferred directions of theta-rhythmic HD cells when an animal enters visually distinct environments.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and a proposed model.

claim: The interaction between non-rhythmic and rhythmic HD cells might contribute to the orientation of grid cells within each grid module.
source: One interesting possibility is that this interaction between non-rhythmic and rhythmic HD cells might contribute to the orientation of grid cells within each grid module (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and previous studies.

claim: Theta-rhythmic and non-rhythmic HD cells could form anatomically distinct populations.
source: Our data suggest that theta-rhythmic and non-rhythmic HD cells could form anatomically distinct populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The differences in spike waveforms indicate that the two populations have distinct intrinsic biophysical properties.
source: The differences in spike waveforms indicate that the two populations have distinct intrinsic biophysical properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of spike waveforms.

claim: Non-rhythmic cells could be preferentially located in the dorsal-most portion of the MEC.
source: Histological analysis also points to the possibility that non-rhythmic cells could be preferentially located in the dorsal-most portion of the MEC.
evidence: This is an inference based on histological analysis.

claim: Non-rhythmic cells could potentially correspond to the large cytochrome-oxidase positive, putatively parasubicular, patches previously described.
source: This could potentially correspond to the large cytochrome-oxidase positive, putatively parasubicular, patches previously described (Burgalossi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on histological analysis and previous studies.

claim: HD cells of the MEC/PaS comprise two functionally distinct types of cells.
source: In conclusion, our results establish that HD cells of the MEC/PaS comprise two functionally distinct types of cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Theta-rhythmic HD cells react coherently when visual landmarks are altered and resemble more closely classic HD cells recorded in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus or presubiculum.
source: Theta-rhythmic HD cells react coherently when visual landmarks are altered and resemble more closely classic HD cells recorded in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus or presubiculum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Non-rhythmic HD cells show larger responses to visual landmark manipulations and respond non-coherently to these manipulations.
source: In contrast, non-rhythmic HD cells not only show larger responses to visual landmark manipulations, but also respond non-coherently to these manipulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: This study reveals the existence of landmark-driven reorganization within a population of HD cells.
source: This study therefore reveals the existence of landmark-driven reorganization within a population of HD cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in the study.

claim: Previous work has shown that non-periodic place selective neurons of the MEC react to alterations in the recording environment by shifting the location of their firing fields.
source: Previous work has shown that non-periodic place selective neurons of the MEC react to alterations in the recording environment by shifting the location of their firing fields (Diehl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An equivalent context-dependent reorganization occurs within the MEC/PaS HD code.
source: The findings presented here indicate that an equivalent context-dependent reorganization occurs within the MEC/PaS HD code.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Each HD cell fires maximally when the head of an animal points in a particular direction, with different cells having different preferred directions.
source: Each HD cell fires maximally when the head of an animal points in a particular direction, with different cells having different preferred directions.
evidence: This is a description of the basic property of HD cells, which is established knowledge.

claim: HD cells are located in both subcortical and cortical areas including the dorsal tegmental nucleus, lateral mammillary nucleus, anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, nucleus reuniens, postsubiculum, retrosplenial cortex, parasubiculum, and the medial entorhinal cortex.
source: HD cells are located in both subcortical and cortical areas including the dorsal tegmental nucleus, lateral mammillary nucleus, anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, nucleus reuniens, postsubiculum, retrosplenial cortex, parasubiculum, and the medial entorhinal cortex (Taube et al., 1990a; Chen et al., 1994; Taube, 1995; Stackman and Taube, 1998; Sharp et al., 2001; Cacucci et al., 2004; Sargolini et al., 2006; Jankowski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The HD signal is generated in subcortical areas, possibly in the dorsal tegmental and lateral mammillary nuclei, and depends on intact vestibular inputs.
source: The HD signal is generated in subcortical areas, possibly in the dorsal tegmental and lateral mammillary nuclei, and depends on intact vestibular inputs (Stackman and Taube, 1997; Muir et al., 2009; Yoder and Taube, 2009; Valerio and Taube, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The HD signal reaches cortical areas via the thalamocortical excitatory projections of the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus.
source: This signal reaches cortical areas via the thalamocortical excitatory projections of the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the HD circuit.

claim: Lesions to the subcortical components of the HD system strongly impair HD representations in cortical areas.
source: Accordingly, lesions to the subcortical components of the HD system strongly impair HD representations in cortical areas (Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Bassett et al., 2007; Winter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Continuous attractor network models provide a mechanistic framework explaining how the HD signal is generated.
source: Continuous attractor network models provide a mechanistic framework explaining how the HD signal is generated (Skaggs et al., 1995; Redish et al., 1996; Zhang, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous computational modeling studies.

claim: In attractor network models, neurons are conceptually arranged in a circle according to their preferred firing direction.
source: In these models, neurons are conceptually arranged in a circle according to their preferred firing direction.
evidence: This is a description of the structure of attractor network models.

claim: The connectivity between any two neurons in attractor network models depends on their relative position.
source: The connectivity between any two neurons depends on their relative position.
evidence: This is a description of the structure of attractor network models.

claim: In attractor network models, neighboring cells with similar preferred HD excite each other, while distant cells tend to inhibit each other.
source: While neighboring cells with similar preferred HD excite each other, distant cells tend to inhibit each other.
evidence: This is a description of the connectivity rules in attractor network models.

claim: This connectivity leads to the emergence of an activity packet which represents the moment-to-moment HD of the animal.
source: This connectivity leads to the emergence of an activity packet which represents the moment-to-moment HD of the animal.
evidence: This is a description of the dynamics of attractor network models.

claim: Attractor network models predict that the differences between the preferred directions of HD cells never change because the connections within the network are immutable.
source: These models predict that the differences between the preferred directions of HD cells never change because the connections within the network are immutable, and most empirical data support this prediction.
evidence: This is a description of a prediction from attractor network models.

claim: Rotation of a distal visual landmark in an environment causes an equivalent rotation of the preferred direction of all HD cells.
source: For example, rotation of a distal visual landmark in an environment causes an equivalent rotation of the preferred direction of all HD cells (Taube et al., 1990b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When distal and proximal cues are rotated in opposite directions, HD cells in the anterior thalamus rotate coherently with one of the two sets of cues.
source: When distal and proximal cues are rotated in opposite directions, HD cells in the anterior thalamus rotate coherently with one of the two sets of cues (Yoganarasimha et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Firing associations of HD cells during exploratory behavior are maintained during sleep.
source: As predicted by the models, firing associations of HD cells during exploratory behavior are maintained during sleep.
evidence: This is a description of findings from previous studies that support attractor network models.

claim: Reliable spike transmission is observed between HD cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and the presubiculum.
source: In addition, reliable spike transmission is observed between HD cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and the presubiculum (Peyrache et al., 2015), suggesting that cortical cells inherit their preferred HD from thalamic HD cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All models of HD cells require a mechanism to anchor the preferred direction of HD cells to the external world, thereby preventing error accumulation inherent to head-movement integration.
source: All models of HD cells require a mechanism to anchor the preferred direction of HD cells to the external world, thereby preventing error accumulation inherent to head-movement integration (Skaggs et al., 1995; Redish et al., 1996; Zhang, 1996; Bicanski and Burgess, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous computational modeling studies.

claim: In attractor network models, the anchoring mechanism involves the interaction between HD cells and cells encoding information about visual landmarks.
source: In these models, the anchoring mechanism involves the interaction between HD cells and cells encoding information about visual landmarks.
evidence: This is a description of the anchoring mechanism in attractor network models.

claim: A subset of directional cells in the retrosplenial cortex are controlled primarily by local visual landmarks, and these cells can change their preferred directions independently of classic HD cells.
source: Recent experimental work has shown that a subset of directional cells in the retrosplenial cortex are indeed controlled primarily by local visual landmarks, and that these cells can change their preferred directions independently of classic HD cells (Jacob et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Cortical regions containing both classic HD cells and cells controlled by visual landmarks might be key sites where visual landmarks gain control over the head direction signal.
source: These observations suggest that cortical regions containing both classic HD cells and cells controlled by visual landmarks might be key sites where visual landmarks gain control over the head direction signal (Goodridge and Taube, 1997; Clark et al., 2010).
